title: Part Squares
context: Grade 5, the pages on the area of irregular shapes and Exercise 8.3. An adult sees a counting rule. What the pages are doing is estimating: whole squares are counted, part squares are rounded to one or to nothing by a rule, and the total is an estimate of the area, not the exact area. A figure drawn along the grid lines has no part squares and needs no estimate.

writeup.why: Estimate the area of a curved or irregular shape on squared paper: number the whole squares, count a square more than half covered as one and leave out one less than half covered, pair the half squares, and give the total with about.
writeup.look: A traced outline on squared paper with every square it touches waiting to be marked, and a tally card at the right that ends on about.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Part Squares' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the number of squares marked. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. The squared paper fills a box 640 by 440 at x 120, y 230, each cell 40 across, with the traced outline in near-black ink. A whole square takes its number in violet, labelled Unit square. A square more than half inside turns rose with the words More than half written in it; a square cut in half turns a paler rose with the word Half; a square less than half inside stays warm white with the words Less than half in small ink. No square is ever marked with a cross. The Pair button stands at x 820, y 250, and a pair is drawn as a thin ink bracket joining two Half squares. The tally card stands at x 820, y 330, 280 by 300, with the lines Whole, More than half, Half pairs and Left out, and a total line that begins with the word about. The estimate reached is green. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys with an sq. cm key. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, and the ten tools of this chapter share them. The lengths the question gives, as a side, a length, a breadth, a height, an edge or a base area, are deep blue, labelled Given or by their own name. The perimeter, area, volume or missing side the working reaches is green, labelled Answer. The boundary that a perimeter walks round is vermilion, labelled Boundary. The unit being counted, one unit square, one unit cube, one row or one layer, is violet, labelled Unit square, Unit cube, Row or Layer. The part squares of an estimate and the space left over where no whole cube fits are rose, labelled More than half, Half or Left over. The side, square, cube, layer or step being worked on now is amber. Grey is kept for a zero holding a place open, and nothing on this stage is ever grey. A square or cube that is not being counted stays warm white inside its near-black outline, grid lines, unit words and signs are near-black ink, and anything dimmed fades to half strength. Chrome never borrows one of them, and each reading survives with the colour taken away, because a part is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The last outline stays with every square marked by its kind, and the tally card beside it ends on about and the area in green.

writeup.delight: On the fourth phase, when the total lands, the word about gives a small bow before it, and the traced hand gives a little wave.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing yet marked. On the first phase a traced leaf lies on squared paper with its whole squares blank. On the second the same leaf's edge squares wait unmarked. On the third a shape lies whose outline cuts squares in half, with the Pair button beside it. On the fourth a traced hand lies with its squares already marked and the tally card waiting. One thing moves, once: the first square to be tapped, or the tally card on the fourth phase, gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line.
writeup.freePlay: Any traced outline, or a figure along the grid lines, marked square by square and tallied. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on whole squares, the rules for part squares, pairing halves and estimates.

source_tool.description: A traced outline is drawn in near-black ink on squared paper, each square 1 cm by 1 cm. The child taps a square to mark its kind, and each tap moves it on through the kinds. A whole square inside the outline takes the next number in violet, labelled Unit square. A square more than half inside turns rose with the words More than half. A square cut exactly in half turns a paler rose with the word Half. A square less than half inside keeps its warm white with the words Less than half in ink, and is left out of the tally. No square is ever marked with a cross. A Pair button joins two Half squares with a bracket and counts them as one whole. A tally card at the right of the working area keeps four lines, Whole, More than half, Half pairs and Left out, and a total line that always begins with about. A number pad types a count or an area in sq. cm. The running count at the top left of the canvas is the number of squares marked.

modes.freePlay: Out of scope here. It is not reached from inside a phase mount, because a phase mount ends idle and has no finish card to reach it from. writeup.freePlay stays as the record of what that activity is, for whoever builds it as its own thing.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: squared paper with equal square cells, rulers marked in centimetres, unit cubes that stack into rows, layers and cuboids, open boxes, and clear jars of water with a level line.
Every figure is drawn to one scale inside its stage, so a side twice as long looks twice as long, and every square cell and every unit cube in one picture is the same size.
Every side, edge and measure carries its unit: cm or m for a length, sq. cm or sq. m for an area, and cu. cm or cu. m for a volume. The longer side of a rectangle is always the one labelled length.
A cuboid is drawn in three visible faces, and a cube only when all its edges are equal. Cubes hidden behind or under others are shown by a see-through layer when they are counted.
A part square on an estimate is marked by its kind, more than half, half or less than half, in words; no cross ever marks a square that is counted.
Nothing is animated except the one thing being explained: a walker tracing a boundary, rows of squares filling a rectangle, layers of cubes stacking into a cuboid, or water rising in a jar.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a square, a cube or a number the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. This chapter colours the roles a measure plays in a piece of working: the lengths the question gives, as a side, a length, a breadth, a height, an edge or a base area, are deep blue, and the perimeter, area, volume or missing side the working reaches is green; those two are the same two in every tool and every picture of this chapter. The boundary that a perimeter walks round is vermilion. The unit being counted, one unit square, one unit cube, one row or one layer, is violet. The part squares an area estimate rounds, and the space left over where no whole cube fits, are rose. The side, square, cube, layer or step being worked on now is amber. Grey is kept for a zero holding a place open and is not used here. A square or cube that is not being counted stays warm white inside its outline, and grid lines and unit words are near-black ink. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Given, Answer, Boundary, Unit square, Unit cube, Layer, More than half, Half and Left over, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Look at that square again. How much of it is inside the line?
voice.onNext: A new shape. Start with the whole squares.
voice.opening: A traced shape on squared paper.
voice.onFinish: You estimated an area, and said about.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Trace any shape and sort its squares.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: More than half or less than half

placement.where: After the class has traced a leaf or a hand on squared paper and coloured the squares by kind. The tool is what sorts every square the outline touches before anything is added, so the rules are seen working one square at a time.

answer_key.rule: Count the whole squares inside the outline first, numbering each one, so none is counted twice. A square more than half covered counts as 1 whole square. A square less than half covered is left out. Two half squares count as 1 whole square. A square cut from corner to corner is cut exactly in half. Add the whole squares, the more-than-half squares and the half squares paired. The total is an estimate, not the exact area, so say about. A figure drawn along the grid lines has no part squares, so its count is its area.
answer_key.wrong: The squares the child marked keep their marks, and the stage outlines the square whose kind is in question in amber and shades how much of it lies inside, so the child can see more or less than half. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked wrong.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: Number each whole square as you count it, row by row.
The rows hold 2, 7, 5 and 4 whole squares.
2 + 7 + 5 + 4 = 18, and the last number written is 18.
So there are 18 whole squares, and none was counted twice.
items.question: A traced leaf has rows of 2, 7, 5 and 4 whole squares. How many whole squares does it hold?
items.checkpoint: Number the whole squares so none is counted twice.
items.misconception: Counting a square again at the start of the next row, because it was not numbered.

steps: A square more than half covered counts as 1 whole square, so the 7 count as 7.
A square less than half covered is left out, so the 3 add nothing.
So these squares add 7 whole squares.
items.question: Round a traced shape, 7 squares are more than half covered and 3 are less than half covered. How many whole squares do they add?
items.checkpoint: More than half counts as one; less than half is left out.
items.misconception: Counting every square the outline touches, which makes the area too big.

steps: Two half squares count as 1 whole square.
Pair them up: 10 half squares make 5 pairs.
items.question: An outline cuts 10 squares exactly in half. How many whole squares do they make?
items.misconception: Counting each half square as a whole one, which counts the halves twice over.

steps: The 6 half squares make 3 whole squares.
21 + 9 + 3 = 33, so the hand is about 33 sq. cm.
Counting squares this way gives an estimate, not the exact area.
items.question: A traced hand has 21 whole squares, 9 more-than-half squares and 6 half squares. What is its area?
items.checkpoint: Say about, because the part squares were rounded.
items.misconception: Calling the count the exact area, though the part squares were only rounded, so it is not exact.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: A traced shape has rows of 3, 6 and 5 whole squares. How many whole squares is that?
A square on the outline is more than half covered. How is it counted?
How many whole squares do 14 half squares make?
items.final_answer: 7, because two half squares make 1 whole square

items.question: Round a traced cup, 9 squares are more than half covered and 5 are less than half covered. How many whole squares do they add?
items.final_answer: 9. The 9 count as 9, and the 5 less-than-half squares are left out

items.question: A square is cut from corner to corner by the outline. How is it counted?
items.final_answer: As a half square, because a cut from corner to corner splits it exactly in half

items.question: A traced leaf has 13 whole squares, 5 more-than-half squares and 4 half squares. What is its area?
items.final_answer: The 4 half squares make 2. 13 + 5 + 2 = 20, so the leaf is about 20 sq. cm

items.question: Is an area found by counting whole and part squares exact? Why?
items.final_answer: No. It is an estimate, because the part squares are rounded to whole squares or left out

items.question: A traced stone has 16 whole squares, 7 more-than-half squares, 6 half squares and 4 less-than-half squares. What is its area?
items.final_answer: The 6 half squares make 3, and the 4 less-than-half squares are left out. 16 + 7 + 3 = 26, so the stone is about 26 sq. cm

practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

teaching_notes: Trace something real, a leaf or a hand, on squared paper before the tool opens. Number the whole squares as they are counted. Mark each part square by its kind, in words or with a letter; a cross is never used for a square that is counted. Two halves make one whole, and a square cut from corner to corner is cut exactly in half. Say about with every answer from counting part squares: it is an estimate, not the exact area. A figure drawn along the grid lines needs no estimate; count every square, or multiply. The printed figures are the child's to count.
